name: Downtown
tagline: Grid blocks, transit lines and the city's tallest towers
description: Salt Lake's enormous 660-foot blocks make Downtown feel wider than it is, but the free-fare TRAX lines, City Creek Center and a dense band of coffee shops around Main Street keep it functional on foot. New glass apartment towers house young professionals and remote workers who want the airport 20 minutes away.
bestFor: Nomads who want to live car-free and be on a train to the ski canyons within the hour.
pros: Free-fare zone on TRAX and buses
Densest cluster of cafes and coworking
cons: Winter inversion traps smog in the valley
Blocks are huge, so walking takes longer than the map suggests
Quiet and hollow after office hours

name: 9th and 9th
tagline: A walkable pocket of indie shops and patio cafes
description: Named for the intersection of 900 South and 900 East, this compact commercial node sits inside a grid of 1920s bungalows. You get a bookshop, a repertory cinema, several strong coffee bars and a bakery all within two blocks, surrounded by tree-shaded streets that stay quiet at night.
bestFor: Remote workers who want a daily cafe routine on foot without living downtown.
pros: Mature street trees and quiet side streets
cons: Rents are high for the size of the units
Bungalow stock means few modern apartments
You still want a car for canyons and errands

name: The Avenues
tagline: Victorian houses stepping up the foothills
description: The city's oldest neighbourhood climbs the bench north of downtown in a grid of narrow lettered and numbered streets lined with restored Victorians and craftsman homes. Trailheads at the top put you on the Bonneville Shoreline within minutes, and the elevation often lifts you above the worst of the winter inversion.
bestFor: Trail runners and hikers who want the mountains at the end of their street.
pros: Often sits above the inversion layer
cons: Steep streets are hard work in snow and ice
Among the priciest rents in the city
Very little in the way of nightlife

name: Sugar House
tagline: The east side's own downtown, minus the office towers
description: Sugar House has its own small commercial core around 1100 East and 2100 South, backed by a large park and a rail-trail bike path running west. Newer mid-rise apartments sit beside older bungalows, and breweries, gyms and grocery stores make it the easiest place in the city to live normally.
bestFor: Longer-stay nomads who want space, a gym and a park rather than downtown density.
pros: Big park plus the S-Line rail trail for cycling
Everything you need without leaving the area
cons: About 15 minutes from downtown by car or tram
Heavy traffic on the main arterials

name: Marmalade and Capitol Hill
tagline: Fruit-tree streets below the State Capitol
description: A small hillside pocket just west of the Capitol, named for the apricot and plum trees that once filled its yards. Streets are narrow and steep with a mix of restored cottages and newer infill townhouses, and you can walk downhill into downtown in about ten minutes.
bestFor: Solo nomads who want downtown proximity but a residential street to come home to.
pros: City and valley views from the upper streets
cons: Limited rentals, it is a small area
Steep walk back up the hill
Almost no bars or restaurants in the pocket itself
